title: Split architecture.md, and drop the mermaid diagrams
body:
`docs/architecture.md` has grown to 423 lines and is now carrying at least three
different kinds of writing for two different readers. PR #17 made this worse by adding
a quantitative argument for the shrink-line guard and a measured error analysis of the
metres frame — both good content, neither of them architecture.

## What is in there now

| Lines | Content | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| 1–30, 93–108 | the two sibling families, composition not subclassing, the per-stencil seam | structure |
| 19–91 | class diagram (mermaid) | diagram |
| 109–169, 250–266 | why `lon_grid`/`lat_grid` is canonical; why lon/lat pairs are keyword-only; why metadata is attached at construction | design decisions |
| 170–249, 267–301 | why tuning parameters are stated in their own units; **why the degeneracy guard is an eigenvalue ratio**; **why the metres frame is equirectangular** | numerical/scientific argument, with measurements |
| 302–353 | "Flow chart: a typical session" (mermaid) | walkthrough |
| 354–409 | "Extracting LCS: shrink lines" | walkthrough |
| 410–423 | reprs | reference |

The two bolded sections are the problem case. They are not decisions about how the code
is *shaped* — they are arguments about what is numerically correct, carrying measured
error tables (eigenvector conditioning vs. relative gap; FTLE error vs. domain latitude
extent; $\det \nabla F$ statistics from the Cabo Verde run). A reader who wants to
convince themselves the science is right has to find them inside a document about class
relationships.

## Proposed split

This lines up with the audience model in `AGENTS.md`. `architecture.md` is addressed to
*the developer*, who needs the design decisions. A document of measured numerical
choices is also for *the inquisitive user* — someone verifying the science without
becoming a developer — which is a different reader and belongs in a different file,
next to `docs/notation.md`.

1. **`docs/architecture.md`** keeps structure, the design decisions, and reprs: what the
   types are and why they are shaped that way.
2. **New `docs/numerics.md`** (name to be settled — `methods.md`?) takes the guard, the
   metres frame, and the tuning-parameter units, with their measurements. These are the
   sections that answer "is this right?" rather than "why is it built like this?".
3. **The two walkthrough sections** (302–409) are the weakest content in the file: they
   re-narrate what the examples already show, for a reader the audience model says reads
   examples rather than `src/`. Fold anything load-bearing into `docs/api.md` and delete
   the rest.

## Drop the mermaid diagrams

Both of them. The architecture is two sibling families with two subclasses each — it
does not need a class diagram, and the sibling-not-inheritance point the diagram exists
to make is already stated in the prose immediately above it. The "typical session" flow
chart restates the four-line quickstart in `README.md`. In practice nobody opens these,
they cost real effort to keep in sync with the code, and a stale diagram is worse than
no diagram.

## Knock-on

`AGENTS.md`, `docs/api.md`, `docs/notation.md` and `plans/review-followup.md` link to
`architecture.md` and need their links updated. `plans/done/seed-flowmap-design.md` also
links to it but is an archived historical record, which `AGENTS.md` explicitly exempts —
leave it.

title: Decide whether ridge selection stays relative (quantile) or gains an absolute option
body:
Step 6 of `plans/review-followup.md` made the tensor-line tuning parameters scale-free:
`window_m` and `line_length_m`/`step_m` are physical lengths, and the termination guard
is the dimensionless `min_anisotropy` ($\lambda_2/\lambda_1$). `AGENTS.md` now carries
that as a binding convention.

`quantile` was deliberately left alone, and it is the one knob that did not get the
treatment. It is a threshold *relative to the field being passed in*, which makes it
scale-free in one sense — 0.90 always means "the top decile" — but it also means the
number of seeds is set by the shape of that particular FTLE distribution rather than by
anything the user asked for. Two runs over the same region with different windows, or
the same window on a smoother field, select different absolute ridge strengths under
the same nominal setting.

Making it absolute changes ridge selection from relative-to-this-field to an absolute
threshold, which is a science decision rather than a units one — which is exactly why
step 6 declined to make it unilaterally.

The question to settle: should ridge selection be relative (`quantile`), absolute (a
floor on the FTLE, in whatever the field's own units are), or should both be available?
Worth deciding alongside any revisit of ridge detection generally.

Deferred out of step 6 of `plans/review-followup.md`. Filed so it survives that plan
being archived.

title: window_m implies a minimum seed spacing of window_m/2, and nothing says so
body:
`ftle_ridge_seeds(window_m=...)` is the ridge-detection scale, and the seed grid has
to resolve it. A window of side `window_m` reaches `window_m / 2` to either side of
its own grid point, so the closest two seeds can be is about **half the window**, not
the window — measured nearest-neighbour ratios run 1.67–1.89 across window sizes.

Nothing computes, enforces, or reports that today. Consequences:

- A user who sets `window_m = 30_000` reasonably expects ~30 km between the tensor
  lines this seeds, and gets ~15 km.
- If the seed grid is too coarse to resolve `window_m`, the rolling window collapses
  toward a single cell and the "local maximum" test stops meaning anything. There is
  no warning.

Options, roughly in increasing order of intrusiveness:

1. Report the implied minimum spacing (and the cell counts actually used) so it is at
   least visible.
2. Warn when `window_m` is smaller than a few grid cells.
3. Redefine the parameter as the minimum seed separation rather than the neighbourhood
   side, so the name matches what the user is choosing. This is the honest fix but
   changes the meaning of an existing default.

Deferred out of step 6 of `plans/review-followup.md`. Filed so it survives that plan
being archived.

title: Allow arbitrary grid-point structure on the auxiliary stencil
body:
`AuxiliarySeed`/`AuxiliaryFlowMap` place four arms (`displacement = [east, north, west,
south]`) around each grid point, and store the grid points themselves as
`lon_grid`/`lat_grid` on the structured `(i, j)` index.

Since the auxiliary stencil makes $\nabla F$ well-defined *per grid point* — it never
differences against neighbouring grid points, only across its own four arms — nothing in
the auxiliary path actually requires the grid points to be laid out on a structured
`(i, j)` mesh. That structure is inherited, not needed.

## Proposal

Allow arbitrary grid-point structure for the auxiliary stencil: a flat list of centres,
a curvilinear mesh, a swath along a ship track, points clustered where the user wants
resolution. The arms and the deformation gradient carry over unchanged; only the
dimension layout changes.

## Scope notes

- The `Neighbor*` classes genuinely do need the structured mesh (they difference against
  `(i ± 1, j ± 1)`), so this is an auxiliary-only relaxation.
- `shrink_lines` currently interpolates the Cauchy-Green tensor on axis-aligned
  `lon_grid`/`lat_grid` axes via `RegularGridInterpolator`, so unstructured centres would
  need a different interpolator there. That is the real cost of this change, not the
  seed side.
- Best combined with the dateline/poleward work (#13) and the metric-frame fix, since all
  three touch how positions are laid out and measured.

Raised in review of #17.

title: Should final products report plain lon/lat instead of lon_grid/lat_grid?
body:
The diagnostic grid coordinates are called `lon_grid`/`lat_grid` throughout, which is
unambiguous inside the package — it separates them from `lon_0`/`lat_0` (reference
release positions) and `lon`/`lat` (advected positions).

But on a *final product* the distinction has served its purpose and the names become
noise. An inquisitive user plotting an FTLE field writes

```python
ftle.plot.pcolormesh(x="lon_grid", y="lat_grid")
```

and gets axes labelled "longitude of the diagnostic grid point" where they wanted
"longitude".

## Question

Should terminal outputs — `ftle()`, `hyperbolic_lcs()`, and friends — rename their grid
coordinates back to plain `lon`/`lat` on the way out, so the internal three-way
distinction stops leaking into the user's plots?

## Tension

- On a `FlowMap`, `lon`/`lat` already mean *advected positions*. Reusing those names on a
  diagnostic output risks the exact collision the three-way split was introduced to
  prevent, and AGENTS.md forbids two different quantities coming back under the same
  `name`.
- On the other hand, a returned FTLE field has no advected positions in it, so within
  that object there is nothing to collide with.

Worth deciding deliberately rather than by default. Raised in review of #17.

title: Deformation gradient uses one cos(phi_ref) for the whole domain
body:
The metres frame `lcs_parcels` computes in is an **equirectangular projection with a
single standard parallel** — not a tangent plane, as the docstrings previously implied:

$$X = R\cos(\phi_{\mathrm{ref}})\,(\lambda - \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}),\qquad Y = R\,(\phi - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}})$$

with $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ the mean of `lat_0`. The **same** frame is used for both the
reference and the advected positions, so $\cos\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ does not cancel
uniformly across the deformation gradient:

$$\nabla F_{\text{true}} = \mathrm{diag}(c_1/c_{\mathrm{ref}},\,1)\;\cdot\;\nabla F_{\text{ours}}\;\cdot\;\mathrm{diag}(c_{\mathrm{ref}}/c_0,\,1)$$

where $c_0 = \cos(\text{release latitude})$, $c_1 = \cos(\text{arrival latitude})$,
$c_{\mathrm{ref}} = \cos(\phi_{\mathrm{ref}})$.

| component | error factor | driven by |
|---|---|---|
| $F_{xx}$ | $c_1/c_0$ | the particle's **meridional excursion** — $c_{\mathrm{ref}}$ cancels exactly |
| $F_{xy}$ | $c_1/c_{\mathrm{ref}}$ | arrival latitude vs domain centre |
| $F_{yx}$ | $c_{\mathrm{ref}}/c_0$ | release latitude vs domain centre |
| $F_{yy}$ | 1 | exact |

## Measured

Same discrete flow map, differenced once in our frame and once with local orthonormal
frames, so only the metric differs:

| domain | lat extent | median FTLE error | p95 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cabo Verde-like | 5° | 0.65 % | 6.0 % |
| basin | 20° | 3.0 % | 25 % |
| hemispheric | 60° | 15 % | 76 % |

Isolating the $c_1/c_0$ term with a rigid meridional translation, which genuinely
squeezes a patch zonally — we report exactly zero:

| translation (7 d window) | true FTLE | ours |
|---|---|---|
| 20°N → 15°N | 0.0039 /day | 0 |
| 45°N → 40°N | 0.0114 /day | 0 |

The first number is 0.8× the shrink-line well-definedness guard it competes with, so
at mid-latitudes the metric error is already the same size as the guard.

## Proposed fix

Exact and cheap — two diagonal rescalings by cosines already present in the dataset:

$$\nabla F = \mathrm{diag}(c_1, 1)\;\cdot\;\frac{\partial(\lambda_1,\phi_1)}{\partial(\lambda_0,\phi_0)}\;\cdot\;\mathrm{diag}(1/c_0, 1)$$

No projection change and no dateline handling required, so this can land independently
of #13 — but it is the same family of problem, so they should be designed together.

Related: #13 (dateline-aware longitude arithmetic).

title: Keyword-only API, canonical grid coords, output metadata and scale-free tensor-line parameters (PR B)
body:
Steps 3–8 of `plans/review-followup.md` — the API and internals half of the PR #7
review follow-up. PR A (#16) landed the audience model and the lint gate; PR C
still owns prose hygiene, the examples rewrite, the data story and CI gating
(steps 9–11), so the plan stays in `plans/`.

## What changed

**3. Keyword-only lon/lat pairs.** Every public entry point that took an adjacent
lon/lat pair now takes it by keyword: `Seed.from_axes` (the ABC and both
overrides), `Seed.pset_to_flowmap`, `FlowMap.image`, `shrink_lines`. A transposed
call is a `TypeError` rather than a plausible answer off the coast of nowhere.
`ftle_ridge_seeds` and `to_parcels_pset` still *return* `(lon, lat)` tuples, so
the `shrink_lines(fm, *ftle_ridge_seeds(ftle))` call form is gone. The convention
is now a rule in `AGENTS.md`.

**4. Canonical `lon_grid`/`lat_grid`.** One name for the diagnostic grid location
on both stencils, replacing `lon_c`/`lat_c` outright. `lon_0`/`lat_0` (release
positions of actual particles) and `lon`/`lat` (advected) are unchanged. The
`_grid_lonlat` helper is gone, and with it both sniffs `AGENTS.md` forbids —
`"displacement" in advected.dims` in `image()` and `"lon_c" in obj.coords`.
Diagnostics no longer carry the `lon_0`/`lat_0` they were differenced from, which
on an `AuxiliaryFlowMap` meant one arm's position labelling an `(i, j)` quantity;
`gradF`/`C`/`ftle` are labelled by `lon_grid`/`lat_grid` only.

**5. Output metadata.** `name`, `long_name`, `units` on every returned array and
on the coordinates. `deformation_gradient()` and `cauchy_green()` no longer come
back under the same name (`_assemble_tensor` hardcoded `"tensor"`). `ftle()` is
1/s. This is what makes vanilla `.plot()` label itself, and what let the
hand-written `* 86400.0` come out of the examples.

**6. Scale-free tuning parameters.** `window` → `window_m` (a distance, converted
to an odd per-dimension cell count from the field's own grid spacing); `n_steps` →
`line_length_m` (it was a line *length* expressed as a step count); and the
degeneracy guard `lambda_max_min` → **`min_anisotropy`**, a floor on
$\lambda_2/\lambda_1$. `quantile` is untouched — making it absolute is a science
decision, not a units one.

The guard took three forms and the two rejected ones are worth recording, since
each was defended on grounds the replacement has to answer. A raw $\lambda_2$
floor retunes with the window: $\lambda_2$ grows exponentially in $|T|$, so a
fixed floor tightens as the window lengthens and a well-definedness guard drifts
into being a selector. A stretching-rate floor in 1/day cures that by dividing out
$|T|$ — but it retunes *worse*, across flow regimes rather than across windows.
Calibrated to the mesoscale ocean at a 7-day window, and measuring each flow
against its own FTLE signal, a fixed 0.005/day is 0.08% for a fast laboratory
flow (FTLE 6/day, $|T|$ = 6 h) and **45.5%** for a slow large-scale one (FTLE
0.011/day, $|T|$ = 180 d); the dimensionless ratio is 2.3% and 1.8% for the same
two. The premise is that $|T|$ is chosen comparable to $1/\mathrm{FTLE}$ of the
flow — which is what an integration window is for.

The ratio retunes with neither, and it is the physically correct quantity rather
than merely the scale-free one: an eigenvector's sensitivity to perturbation of
$C$ scales as the inverse of the *relative* eigenvalue gap, so
$\lambda_2/\lambda_1$ is exactly what decides whether $\xi_1$ is a direction or
numerical noise. Measured — at 1.15 a 1% error in $C$ swings $\xi_1$ by about 2
degrees, at 1.05 by 6 degrees, and by a ratio of 4 it has flattened at 0.25
degrees. `|T|` leaves `shrink_lines` entirely, and `SECONDS_PER_DAY` with it.

The default 1.15 reproduces the old behaviour at the calibration point to 0.012%:
at 7 days, 0.005/day corresponded to a $\lambda_2$ floor of 1.0725, which for
incompressible flow is a ratio of 1.15.

**Away from that point it is not cosmetic, because the ocean surface is not
incompressible.** Measured on the Cabo Verde example (5-day window, points taken
34 km clear of any coast), the areal factor $\det \nabla F$ has a median of 1.08
forward and 0.97 backward but ranges 0.63–2.4 forward and 0.045–14 backward; the
implied divergence reaches 0.08–0.13 /day at p99 against a median FTLE of about
0.13 /day — the same order as the signal. On the backward flow the old
$\lambda_2$ floor terminates 0.97% of grid points against the ratio floor's
0.135%, and the **78 points it kills alone have a median $\det \nabla F$ of 0.75
with a median ratio of 1.6** — strongly convergent, with $\xi_1$ perfectly well
defined. A magnitude floor cannot tell "nothing is stretching here" from
"everything is contracting here", so it preferentially terminates shrink lines
inside convergence zones — which is where attracting LCS live. Forward, where the
median areal factor exceeds 1, the two guards agree closely at the window
measured, which is why the bias never surfaced during forward-only development.

**7. Tensor-line internals.** `xi1`/`step`/`half` and the nested
`central_diff`/`arm_diff` are lifted to tested module-level functions with names
that say what they do (`_shrink_line_tangent`, `_step_lonlat_by_meters`,
`_trace_half_line`, `_central_diff`, `_arm_diff`). `_shrink_line_tangent`
documents that it returns NaN wherever the tangent is not well defined — off the
grid, in a NaN cell, or below the guard being one condition with three causes, so
a caller need not know which fired. Documented sharp edges: RK2, the heading flip,
the 45-degree initial-branch tie-break, the midpoint degeneracy guard, and the
fixed line length as NaN-fill with a pointer to #11.

**8. Reprs and `FlowMap.hyperbolic_lcs()`.** Terse one-line summaries on
`Seed`/`FlowMap` (`.ds` is still how you get the dataset). The repr reports the
signed `T` and stops there: repelling/attracting is a property of the diagnostic,
not of the flow map, and printing a signed window *and* a direction word was
redundant. `hyperbolic_lcs()` — named for the family, since #8 will add elliptic
LCS — computes the FTLE once and hands it to `ftle_ridge_seeds`, which keeps
taking the field rather than the `FlowMap`, so no hidden recomputation and no
duplicated ridge logic. It documents that each call recomputes a potentially
expensive FTLE.

## Corrections to things the code or docs claimed

- **The metres frame is not a tangent plane.** It is an equirectangular projection
  with a *single* standard parallel at the mean of `lat_0`, and the same frame
  carries both reference and advected positions, so $\cos\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ does
  not cancel uniformly:
  $\nabla F_{\text{true}} = \mathrm{diag}(c_1/c_{\mathrm{ref}}, 1)\,\nabla F_{\text{ours}}\,\mathrm{diag}(c_{\mathrm{ref}}/c_0, 1)$.
  $F_{yy}$ is exact, $F_{xx}$ is off by $c_1/c_0$ (driven by meridional excursion —
  $c_{\mathrm{ref}}$ cancels there), off-diagonals by $c_1/c_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and
  $c_{\mathrm{ref}}/c_0$. For one analytic test flow map the median FTLE error runs
  0.65% / 3.0% / 15% over 5- / 20- / 60-degree domains — an illustration of scale,
  not a property of the frame indexed by domain width; the driver is meridional
  excursion relative to the standard parallel. A rigid meridional translation from
  20°N to 15°N has a true FTLE of 0.0039 /day and we report exactly zero. Named
  correctly throughout, stated as a scope limit in the README, filed as #18.
- **`line_length_m` is a cap**, not the achieved length; a line that terminates
  early is shorter.
- **`window_m` is the neighbourhood side**, so the closest two seeds can be is
  about `window_m / 2` — the docs implied `window_m`. (The bound is geometric: the
  window reaches `window_m / 2` to either side of its own grid point.)
- **"Haller–Sapsis duality" was our coinage**, not a community term. Now
  "forward–backward duality", citing Haller & Sapsis 2011,
  [doi:10.1063/1.3579597](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.3579597).
- **`_assemble_tensor`'s rename rationale was false.** It claimed the four
  per-component renames stopped `xarray.concat` dropping one; `concat` on
  differently-named arrays silently keeps the first name, and the components arrive
  with `name=None` anyway. Renames dropped, result verified `.identical()` to before.
- **Both LCS notebooks still claimed in their intro cells that they "run offline"**,
  which 9f78118 fixed in the Currents cells but missed.
- **Seven pseudo-signature blocks were fenced as `python`** though a bare `->`
  outside a `def` is a syntax error. Now `text`. `\operatorname` → `\mathrm`.

## Other internals

- **No in-place xarray mutation** anywhere in `src/` — every `attrs.update` /
  `attrs[...] =` rebuilt functionally, since pandas has removed nearly all its
  in-place operations and xarray may follow. Pinned by a test that deep-copies
  `fm.ds`, runs the whole diagnostic chain and asserts identity.
- **`NeighborFlowMap.deformation_gradient`** inlines its central differences, so a
  reader is not left parsing `reference_step_x` as `dx` when a centred difference
  spans `2*dx`.
- **`given()` → `_filter_kwargs()`**, documenting why: a forwarded `None` would push
  the sentinel into the public signatures of `ftle_ridge_seeds`/`shrink_lines`,
  which would each then have to resolve it. Filtering keeps one home per default.
- **The deferred `tensorlines` import** in `hyperbolic_lcs` is now documented as the
  deliberate remedy for a real layering inversion, bought for the one-call ergonomics.
- **New `AGENTS.md` conventions**, each derived from a review comment: no in-place
  xarray mutation; repeated attribute sets become module constants; a notebook
  references only notebooks of lower rank (rank order recorded); tuning parameters
  are scale-free, and "physical" is not sufficient.
- **New `examples/README.md`** with the reading order, the jupytext contract and the
  currents-file prerequisite.

## Adversarial verification

Six refuters, each attacking one area by running code, with every claimed defect
then attacked by an independent counter-refuter. Two areas survived intact
(migration completeness; the examples). The rest found real problems, all now
fixed:

- **A regression this PR introduced.** `FlowMap.image()` raised `MergeError`
  whenever the caller's `lon0`/`lat0` carried dims named `lon`/`lat` — i.e.
  `grid["lon"], grid["lat"]` off any ordinary CF dataset, the most natural way to
  call it. The no-in-place-mutation rewrite caused it: `assign()` merges, and a
  merge cannot tell an incoming data variable `lon` from a dimension of the same
  name. Rebuilt with an explicit `xr.Dataset`; verified against the pre-PR
  implementation that previously-failing inputs now work and previously-working
  inputs are `.identical()`.
- **Two guard parameters were unpinned.** The `min_anisotropy` *default* could be
  lowered to 1.0 — silently disabling the guard for every default-path caller —
  and `hyperbolic_lcs` could stop forwarding it, both with the suite fully green.
- **Documentation errors:** tensor dims documented as `(i, j, row, col)` when they
  ship as `('row','col','i','j')` and `('row','i','j','col')`; the FTLE written
  with `1/(t_1 - t_0)` where the code uses `1/|T|`, which differs for the backward
  maps this package exists to support; the symbol table omitting the auxiliary
  `displacement` dim; and `min_anisotropy <= 1` being a silent no-op (for PSD `C`,
  `lambda_2 >= lambda_1`, so the guard can never fire) with nothing saying so.
- **Four overclaimed measurements of mine.** The seed-spacing ratio 1.67–1.89 came
  from one synthetic uniform-random field and does not reproduce on the real Cabo
  Verde fields — deleted outright, since the bound that matters is geometric and
  needs no measurement. The metric-error percentages, the rate-vs-ratio table and
  the forward-flow agreement are now attributed to the flow map, premises and
  window they came from.

body:
PR A of the PR #7 review follow-up — see `plans/review-followup.md`. The
contract only: no API or example changes, those are PR B and C.

## The audience model

`AGENTS.md` gains an `## Audience` section naming three readers — the trusting
user, the inquisitive user verifying the science without becoming a developer,
and the developer who needs the design *decisions*. The example and notebook
rules are rewritten as derivations of it. New rules that fall out:

- explain the non-obvious choice; do not re-teach the field — while still
  defining a term properly where it is ambiguous;
- examples prefer explicit, duplicated code over indirection — library code does
  not;
- every returned xarray data array carries `name`, `long_name`, `units`, in SI
  (the precondition for vanilla plots in PR C);
- reader-facing text carries no process narrative or design rationale.

The vanilla-plot rule is clarified: it governs the plot you *first write*, and
is anti-over-styling rather than a ban on ever passing a keyword — the review
sweep misread it as a rule the LCS examples violate wholesale. The
moved-plan-link exemption is narrowed to docs and plans; `src/` and `tests/`
should not link plans at all (the two existing violations are removed in step
9). A merge rule is added as well: PRs land squashed onto a linear `main`, so
the PR body is the commit message and its `Closes` references do the closing.

## Ruff

Lands early so the PR B and C diffs stay reviewable. `pixi run lint` is
`ruff check` plus `ruff format --check`, gated by a new CI job. Selects `I`,
`UP`, `B`, `NPY`, `RUF`; ignores the ambiguous-unicode rules, since the prose
uses en dashes deliberately; excludes generated `.ipynb`/`.md` and the vendored
`.claude` skills; ignores `E402`/`B018` in the example `.py` sources, where
cell-level imports and a bare `ds` to display it are the notebook idiom.

The 21 findings were mechanical — import sorting, `dict()` to literals,
`zip(..., strict=True)`. One formatter result was worse than its input
(`tensorlines.py` broke `d[:, 1]` across three lines) and became two named
locals instead. The example notebooks were re-synced after formatting with
their cell outputs intact, so nothing needed re-executing against CMEMS.

## Example touch-up

The `ParticleSet` construction folds onto one line in all three advecting
examples: Parcels v4 broadcasts a scalar `t` over the particle count
(`particleset.py:99`), so the `np.full(len(lon), t0)` array was never needed.
`z` has no such broadcast — it is asserted to match `x.size` — so it moves to
its own line. `z=None` would drop the array entirely but resolves to
`min(0, depth[0])`, i.e. 0.0 rather than the field's first level, so it is not
the same seeding depth. Untested against a real fieldset; it proves out when
the examples execute in PR C.

title: Q3: instantaneous OECS from the rate-of-strain tensor (and the tensor-line refactor it forces)
body:
Surveyed as Approach C in `plans/done/lcs-time-evolution.md`; deferred there when Q1 was chosen. Filing so the deferred content is tracked outside the archived plan.

**Question.** What is the *instantaneous* coherent structure at each moment? The short-time limit of an LCS is an Objective Eulerian Coherent Structure (OECS; Serra & Haller 2016, [doi:10.1063/1.4951720](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4951720)), computed from the rate-of-strain tensor $S = \tfrac{1}{2}(\nabla v + \nabla v^\top)$ at a single instant — no window, naturally a frame per snapshot.

**Why it is attractive.** No advection at all: $\nabla v$ comes straight off the gridded velocity via xarray. It is by far the cheapest route to a time-evolution movie, and carries no tracking heuristics (contrast #14).

**The real payload is a refactor, not a feature.** Hyperbolic OECS are the *same* tensor-line integration we already have, with $S$ in place of $C$, and its smaller/larger eigenvalue selecting attracting/repelling. `shrink_lines` currently pulls $C$ out of a `FlowMap`. The reusable core is "integrate tensor lines of a symmetric 2-tensor field, seeded at eigenvalue extrema" — factoring that out lets one integrator serve both finite-time LCS (from $C$) and instantaneous OECS (from $S$).

That makes this an API decision as much as a feature, and it interacts with the tensor-line work in the PR #7 review follow-up (parameters in physical units, lifting the nested helpers to tested top-level functions) and with #11 (output structure).

**Caveat.** Instantaneous, not finite-time: OECS approximate LCS only over short horizons. This answers "how do the instantaneous structures evolve", not "how does one finite-time LCS move".

**Open questions.**

- Where to compute $\nabla v$ — on the native CMEMS grid or a resampled one, and how sensitive OECS are to that choice.
- Is `tensor_lines(tensor_field, seeds)` (with `shrink_lines` and an `oecs_*` wrapper on top) the right seam, or premature generality before OECS is actually attempted?

References: Serra, M. & Haller, G. (2016). *Objective Eulerian coherent structures.* Chaos 26:053110. [doi:10.1063/1.4951720](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4951720).

title: Q2: sliding-window LCS re-extraction and frame-to-frame tracking
body:
Surveyed as Approach B in `plans/done/lcs-time-evolution.md`; deferred there when Q1 was chosen. Filing so the deferred content is tracked outside the archived plan.

**Question.** How does the LCS *skeleton itself* evolve — how do ridges appear, disappear, merge, and split as the analysis window slides? This is distinct from Q1 (where a given material curve goes), which is shipped.

**Shape.** For release times $t_0^{(k)} = t_0 + k\Delta$ at fixed window $T$, compute forward and backward shrink lines at each, giving a sequence of LCS frames; then link curves between consecutive frames into tracks.

Correspondence options, increasing sophistication:

1. Curve proximity — modified Hausdorff distance between polylines, match under a threshold.
2. Mask overlap — rasterise each LCS to a thin mask, match by intersection-over-union (the workhorse of ocean-eddy tracking).
3. Predictive — advect frame-$k$ seeds by $\Delta$ and match predictions to frame-$k{+}1$ seeds/curves. Overlapping windows already share flow history, which stabilises continuity.

**What exists.** Frame *generation* is essentially supported: a release series is `flowmap.to_seed()` then `pset_to_flowmap(..., t0=..., t1=...)` per window. The tracking is new logic, but can lean on `scipy.spatial` (KD-trees, directed Hausdorff) and `scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment`.

**Cost.** Each frame is a full advection ($N$ windows x two directions), so this is the expensive branch.

**Open questions.**

- How long a window $T$ and step $\Delta$, and how much window overlap is worth the extra compute for cleaner tracks?
- What does "the same LCS across frames" operationally mean when ridges merge or split — track curves, or the underlying seeds/ridge points?
- Validation: the periodically forced double gyre is the standard LCS benchmark and should anchor this before it is trusted on CMEMS. Is there also an observational check (drifter clusters, altimetry eddies) the group already trusts?

References: Haller (2015), [doi:10.1146/annurev-fluid-010313-141322](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-fluid-010313-141322).

title: Longitude arithmetic is not dateline-aware (means, diffs, metric frame)
body:
Deferred from the PR #7 review.

Every place we do arithmetic on longitudes treats them as a plain real line. Across the antimeridian (and, separately, near the poles) that is wrong: a difference between $-179$ and $+179$ comes out as $-358$ instead of $+2$, and an arithmetic mean of the two lands at $0$ instead of $180$.

Known sites (not exhaustive — the sweep should be part of the fix):

- `FlowMap.image` / the auxiliary centre — `advected.mean("displacement", skipna=False)` in `src/lcs_parcels/grids.py:456`. Arithmetic mean of longitudes.
- `_reference_lonlat` (`grids.py:93-95`) — `float(lon_0.mean())` for the metric-frame anchor.
- `_to_meters` / `_lonlat_to_meters` (`grids.py:106-111`) — `lon - lon_ref` unwrapped.
- `NeighborFlowMap.deformation_gradient` — the nested `central_diff` differencing `lon`.
- `AuxiliaryFlowMap.deformation_gradient` — the nested `arm_diff` differencing `lon` across arms.
- `tensorlines.py:123` — `lat_ref = float(flowmap.ds["lat_0"].mean())`, and the stepping at `tensorlines.py:148-150` advances `lon` with no wrap.

The single `cos(phi_ref)` metric frame is a related but distinct approximation: it degrades with domain size and latitude, and is undefined at the poles.

Scope to decide when this is picked up:

- A shared longitude-difference helper (wrap to $(-180, 180]$) plus a circular-mean helper, used everywhere instead of raw `-` and `.mean()`.
- Whether to normalise longitudes on ingest instead, or carry a branch-cut convention on the dataset.
- Whether the metric frame stays a single-cosine tangent plane or becomes something dateline- and pole-safe.
- Tests seeded across the antimeridian and at high latitude — none exist today.

Not blocking the review PR: every current example is in the Cabo Verde region, far from the antimeridian, so nothing is visibly wrong yet.

title: LCS time evolution: evolve extracted LCS as material curves
body:
**Stacked on #5** (base = `feature/hyperbolic-lcs-tensorlines`).

Implements Q1 of the time-evolution plan: an extracted hyperbolic LCS is a
**material** curve, so its later position is fixed by the flow,
$\mathcal{M}(t) = F_{t_0}^{t}(\mathcal{M}(t_0))$ (Haller 2015 Eq. 5). We evolve it
by *interpolating* a captured flow map at the curve's vertices — no second
integrator, self-consistent with the map that diagnosed it.

### Package
- **`FlowMap.image(lon0, lat0) -> xr.Dataset`** — apply the stored flow map to
  arbitrary reference points; vectorized and dim-preserving over the
  `(line, point)` grid `shrink_lines` returns. Works on both stencils (auxiliary
  advected centre = arm centroid); off-grid / NaN inputs map to NaN. Reads the
  diagnostic axes through a shared `_grid_lonlat` helper (now in `grids.py`).
- `tests/test_evolution.py` — node exactness, off-node linear interpolation, dim
  preservation, off-grid/NaN, and the auxiliary layout.

### Example
`examples/cabo_verde_lcs_evolution` (executed, offline): advect the grid to a few
horizons per direction, diagnose the LCS at the longest, and evolve each family
in its **coherent** direction (attracting forward, repelling backward). A
cross-check against a direct Parcels advection of the same vertices agrees to
**median 0.20 km** (max 5.6 km) over the 5-day window.

### Design note
The plan's tidy "chunk one advection and snapshot each $\Delta$" mechanism is
**unsafe with the NaN recovery kernel**: once a particle is recovered to NaN, that
NaN persists into the next `execute` and stalls the whole set's time stepping, so
later chunks silently no-op. Replaced by one single-shot advection per horizon —
a few extra advections, but each map is a validated flow map. Documented in
`plans/lcs-evolution-q1.md`.

Q2 (sliding-window tracking) and Q3 (OECS) remain deferred.

title: Hyperbolic LCS as strain tensor lines, with material-curve evolution
body:
## What

Constructs **repelling and attracting LCS as strain tensor lines** (Haller 2015,
§5.1 / Table 1, $n=2$;
DOI [10.1146/annurev-fluid-010313-141322](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-fluid-010313-141322)),
and evolves an extracted LCS as a material curve — both a package API and example
notebooks. The time-evolution layer (stacked PR #6) has been merged into this
branch.

## Package API (`lcs_parcels.tensorlines` + `FlowMap.image`)

```python
from lcs_parcels import ftle_ridge_seeds, shrink_lines

repelling  = shrink_lines(forward,  *ftle_ridge_seeds(forward.ftle()))
attracting = shrink_lines(backward, *ftle_ridge_seeds(backward.ftle()))
```

- A repelling LCS is a **shrink line** tangent to $\xi_1$; attracting LCS are the
  shrink lines of the **backward** flow (Haller–Sapsis duality), so it is just
  *which* `FlowMap` you pass. `shrink_lines` returns polylines on `(line, point)`.
- Free functions keep the new dep (`scipy`) at the boundary; the ODE loop is the
  one place we leave label-based xarray.
- **`FlowMap.image(lon0, lat0)`** applies a captured flow map to arbitrary points,
  so an extracted LCS is evolved by interpolating a flow map at its vertices —
  vectorized, dim-preserving, both stencils, off-grid/NaN → NaN.

## Example notebooks (executed)

- `cabo_verde_lcs` — repelling/attracting LCS over their FTLEs (offline, bundled
  currents).
- `cabo_verde_lcs_evolution` — evolve each family in its coherent direction;
  cross-checked against a direct Parcels advection of the same vertices to
  **median 0.20 km** over the 5-day window.
- `cabo_verde_ftle` — the FTLE from live CMEMS.

## Correctness fixes from review

- `shrink_lines` now steps in the **single-reference-latitude** metric its tensor
  is diagnosed in (was a per-point `cos(lat)`, bowing curves ~2.5% at the edges).
- `FlowMap.image` on auxiliary grids returns NaN when a stencil arm is lost (was a
  biased centroid). `FlowMap.ftle()` no longer leaks a scalar `eig` coord.
- Both with regression tests. **46 tests pass**; lint clean; both pixi envs
  install `--locked` on linux/macOS/Windows; Parcels pinned to a v4 git SHA.

## Notes for reviewers

The example plots keep a grey FTLE backdrop under colored LCS lines and per-panel
family titles — a deliberate departure from the vanilla-plot default, since the
overlay and the two-family contrast are the point.

title: Add real CMEMS/Parcels Cabo Verde forward-FTLE example
body:
## What

An end-to-end LCS example: forward FTLE around the **Cabo Verde** archipelago from **CMEMS** hourly surface currents, advected with **Parcels v4**, computed with **both** `lcs_parcels` stencils (neighbor and auxiliary).

`examples/cabo_verde_ftle.py` (+ synced `.md`/`.ipynb`, executed with outputs):
download & cache a CMEMS subset → build a Parcels v4 `FieldSet` → advect the 0.1°-family seed grid 10 d forward (RK4, hourly step) → ingest advected positions into `FlowMap`s → shade the FTLE. All tunables (release time, window, **resolution**, stencil arm length, domain) live in a papermill `parameters` cell; default resolution is **1/25°**.

At 1/25° the two stencils agree closely (both mean ≈ 0.107 /day; max 0.34 vs 0.37 /day), resolving the same web of repelling-LCS ridges around the islands. ~7.8 % of particles ground on land / leave the domain and surface as `NaN`.

## Environment

- Parcels v4 (alpha) pinned to a `main` git **SHA** in a dedicated **`examples`** pixi env (Python 3.13 + `copernicusmarine` + matplotlib).
- Default env kept **minimal** and pinned to **Python 3.13** (newest Parcels v4 supports) so `pixi run test` runs on a Parcels-compatible interpreter. All 33 core tests pass.
- Run the example with `pixi run -e examples jupytext --sync --execute examples/cabo_verde_ftle.py`.

## Docs

- `AGENTS.md`: pixi env conventions (CLI-driven changes, the minimal/examples split) and the Parcels v4 loading/advection recipe (sgrid `FieldSet`, `x`/`y` positions, NaN-recovery kernel).
- `README.md`: pointer to the new example.
